  DATE: January 17, 2024
  AGENDA ITEM NO:  Old Business - 2A

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Jessica Serrano, Director of Community Development
 SUBJECT:  Discussion of Findings on City’s Inclusionary Housing Ordinance
  Feasibility/Fee Study

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and filing the report and presentation;
  2. Providing direction to staff; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On September 6, 2023, the City Council adopted an Inclusionary Housing Ordinance
(IHO) and an IHO in-lieu fee formula. As part of this action, Council also directed the City
Manager to conduct an evaluation of the City’s IHO to determine whether it is financially
feasible and recommend in-lieu fees in cases where an IHO is feasible. Based on the
Council’s direction, the City partnered with the San Gabriel Valley Council of
Governments (SGVCOG), and was able to participate in SGVCOG’s sub-regional effort
to provide technical assistance addressing affordable housing issues. The City entered
into an agreement with the SGVCOG, for its consultant, Economic & Planning Systems
(EPS), to conduct an IHO feasibility study tailored to Monterey Park.

EPS’s feasibility study is intended to inform and educate the City Council on the potential
effects of the IHO on future residential development in the City. The study’s overall
conclusion states that the requirements of the IHO are likely to be financially challenging
for new residential development within the City and may constrain new projects.

BACKGROUND:
The City adopted the 2021-2029 Housing Element of the General Plan on January 19,
2022; it was certified by the California Department of Housing and Community
Development on March 20, 2023. Housing Element Program 15 provides that the City
Council will consider an inclusionary housing program. Such programs require certain
residential and mixed-use developments to designate a percentage of units within the
development as affordable housing. Alternatively, a developer may construct off-site
units, or pay a fee or dedicate land in the City for the creation of affordable units.

To implement Program 15 of the Housing Element, the Council began consideration of

an IHO in Fall of 2022. The IHO was ultimately approved on September 6, 2023. Along
with the IHO, a formula to provide for developers the option to pay an in-lieu fee rather
than construct units on-site was also adopted. This formula requires the developer to pay
the “affordability gap,” which represents the gap between the market-rate price (sales or
rent) and the affordable price (sales or rent) of the inclusionary unit.

Drawing on local research and input from City representatives, EPS developed several
building prototypes representative of development patterns in the City, and assessed how
the City’s IHO and in-lieu fee formula would affect the different prototype developments.
The assessment utilized data on typical construction and land costs and rents and sales
prices for recently-built housing projects in the City and the larger San Gabriel Valley
subregion. The data allowed EPS to evaluate how likely a developer would be to pursue
the construction of the modeled prototypes, based on industry standard financial
feasibility metrics. The evaluation modeled the financial feasibility for the prototypes under
three different assumptions:

  1. That they are rented or sold completely at market rents/sale prices;
  2. That they include the affordable units required by the IHO; and
  3. That they pay an in-lieu fee aligned with the requirements of the IHO (i.e., based
  on the “affordability gap”).

The findings of the analysis generally indicate that the financial impacts of the City’s IHO
and in-lieu fee formula may dampen new residential development in the City.

ANALYSIS
In conducting its analysis, EPS created prototype developments that reflect future
development types based on existing zoning and recent development trends. The
prototypes are listed below and are categorized either as development seen in:

City-wide - traditional residential areas:
  • Single Family Attached Townhome
  • Multi-Family Condominium
  • Multi-Family Rental

City’s Mixed-Use Downtown corridor:
  • Multi-Family Condominium
  • Multi-Family Rental – More Parking
  • Multi-Family Rental – Less Parking

The modeling of the various prototypes showed that the single family attached townhome
prototype meets industry-standard development feasibility thresholds at market rates and
could feasibly support the requirements of the City’s inclusionary housing requirements.
All other modeled prototypes were found to be financially challenged even at market
rates, and therefore would be unlikely to support the additional costs of the City’s
inclusionary housing requirements. This condition may in turn dampen future residential

 Staff Report
Page 3 of 4
January 17, 2024

development in the City as developers may find it challenging to absorb the cost of either
setting aside affordable units or paying an equivalent in-lieu fee, particularly for multi-
family rental and ownership projects.

EPS additionally calculated an in-lieu fee for the modeled prototypes that would represent
the equivalent cost that developers would bear if the inclusionary housing requirements
were met on-site. The calculation approach used by EPS is slightly different than the one
detailed in the City’s adopted in-lieu fee formula, but still meets the goal of setting a fee
that reflects the financial impact of the IHO requirements.

Based on the study conducted, there are implementation considerations to help achieve
the creation of affordable units while not inhibiting the creation of market rate units.
Potential strategies to better implement the IHO include:

  •  Temporarily pause the IHO requirements and monitor market conditions;
  •  Adjust IHO requirements for projects to automatically qualify for State Density
  Bonus;
  •  Adopt an In-Lieu Fee lower than equivalent cost of providing units on-site; and/or
  •  Phase-in the IHO requirements over a set time period.

Without some of the measures indicated above, and in today’s housing market, most
housing developers in the City will not be able to realistically support the costs associated
with the provision of affordable housing as required by the current IHO.

2023-2024 STRATEGIC PLAN GOAL:
The IHO feasibility study helps implement the Program 15 of the Housing Element, which
included the creation of an IHO and helps address the City Council’s Housing goal in the
2023-24 strategic plan. In-lieu fees will offer options for a developer to comply with the
IHO and may help with the maintenance and creation of affordable housing units within
the City.

FISCAL IMPACT:
There are no identifiable fiscal impacts associated with the presentation of findings of the
IHO feasibility study.

1. Introduction

Study Background
The City of Monterey Park (City) adopted an Inclusionary Housing Ordinance
(IHO) in August 2023 and it became effective in September 2023. Inclusionary
housing ordinances require that new market-rate residential development projects
include a certain percentage of housing units at rents or sale prices that are
affordable to lower-income households. Per the City’s IHO, developers of new
residential projects are required to provide 15 percent of the new units built as
affordable to lower-income households. For rental developments, the 15 percent
requirement consists of 9 percent of units affordable to households earning the
Low-Income level for Los Angeles County and 6 percent of units affordable to
households earning the Moderate Income level. For ownership developments, 15
percent of units are required to be affordable to households earning the Moderate
Income level. 1 The IHO also includes an option for developers to pay a fee in-lieu
of providing affordable units on-site as an alternative means of compliance.

Following adoption of the IHO, the City sought to study how the ordinance could
impact the financial feasibility of new market-rate housing developments in the
City. Additionally, the City wanted to consider a more standardized and
transparent approach to the in-lieu fee formula included in the IHO. The current
formula requires the developer to uniquely calculate the gap between the value of
their project’s market-rate units and the value of the required affordable units,
and leaves room for interpretation regarding the calculation of unit value, which
can fluctuate on a variety of factors such as unit size, type, market conditions,
and more.

Economic & Planning Systems, Inc. (EPS) was retained by the San Gabriel Valley
Council of Governments (SGVCOG) on behalf of the City to conduct a feasibility
analysis of the IHO and to calculate potential in-lieu fee levels that are consistent
with the IHO’s on-site unit requirement. The feasibility analysis specifically tests
whether new market-rate residential developments in the City can absorb the
additional financial costs associated with the IHO requirements and still be
financially feasible. While cities are generally not legally required to consider the
financial impacts of an inclusionary housing requirement, the City has elected
to study them to better inform its inclusionary housing policy and align the City’s
overall housing goals with its local real estate market conditions. 2

Inclusionary Housing Economic Feasibility Evaluation

Overview of Feasibility Analysis
The financial feasibility of a development project is determined by comparing the
cost of the project to its value (based on achievable sale prices or rents).
A financially feasible project is one in which the value provides a sufficient return
on the investment to incentivize moving forward with the project. Given the range
of investment opportunities available to developers and financial investors,
a development project will not be built if it is not considered a financially feasible
proposition. For the purposes of this study’s analysis, a “sufficient” return on
investment was established using market-based standards that are relevant
at the time of this analysis (further detailed in Chapter 3). However, what is
considered a “sufficient” return for any individual project will vary depending on
a range of considerations.

The impacts of inclusionary housing policies on the financial feasibility of market-
rate housing projects can manifest in one of two ways:

1. On-site inclusionary affordable units typically cost the same to build as the
  market-rate units but are sold or rented at below-market rates; OR
2. Fees paid in-lieu of providing affordable units on-site add to the costs of a
  project, while the value of the project as reflected in market-rate rents or sale
  prices tends to stay the same.

The resulting decrease in project revenue or increase in development costs
related to inclusionary policies will reduce the achievable return on investment for
housing projects. At a certain level, the impacts of the policy may reduce the
achievable return to the point that projects are financially infeasible, and
developers will not move forward with building them. This study is intended to
provide the City with additional context regarding the cost associated with its
inclusionary requirement and whether it might render new residential
development in the City extremely challenging or even completely financially
infeasible. This context is important given that the production of affordable units
through an inclusionary housing policy can only happen through the development

Key Findings and Recommendations
The key findings and recommendations stemming from the feasibility analysis for
inclusionary housing in Monterey Park are summarized below. It is important to
note that the analysis is a point-in-time assessment of typical new market-rate
development projects completed in late 2023. The findings are not deterministic
of all development feasibility in the City, as there are many variables that can
impact costs and values and resulting feasibility of any individual project.
Similarly, future market conditions can also change the financial forces impacting
real estate development generally and inclusionary housing programs specifically.

1. Higher-density owner- and renter-occupied residential projects
  appear financially challenging to build in the City, while lower-density
  owner-occupied projects appear financially feasible. The feasibility
  analysis indicates that the development of higher density residential products,
  such as multifamily owner-occupied condominiums and renter-occupied
  apartments, appear financially infeasible even at market rates. By contrast,
  lower density residential products such as owner-occupied attached
  townhomes appears to be feasible at market rates, and demonstrate sufficient
  development feasibility to absorb the additional impact of an inclusionary
  requirement.

2. The zoning allowances under the City’s Mixed-Use (MU) zoning
  designation may improve the financial feasibility of residential
  projects. Residential projects in the MU zoned areas of the City generate a
  higher return on investment than development in other parts of the City due
  to the MU zone’s unlimited density allowances and lower parking
  requirements. However, in order for future projects in the MU zone to support
  the additional cost of inclusionary units, they would likely need to achieve
  even higher densities and lower parking ratios than the MU pipeline projects
  currently proposed.

3. The City’s current inclusionary housing requirements will likely be
  financially challenging for new residential development projects under
  current market conditions. This challenge is particularly seen for
  multifamily residential rental and ownership projects, which are facing other
  financial challenges related to development costs and achievable market
  rates. Chapter 5 of this report outlines a number of options the City may
  consider to improve the efficacy of the IHO in developing affordable units in
  the community while also supporting new residential development overall.

The subsequent chapters of this report detail on the methodology, key
assumptions, and results of the feasibility analysis, as well as the calculation of an
in-lieu fee aligned with the City’s current IHO requirements.

3. Development Feasibility Analysis
The development feasibility analysis detailed in this study tests whether new
market-rate residential development in the City can absorb the financial impact of
an inclusionary housing requirement. This assessment reflects that building
affordable housing units represents a cost to market-rate housing projects, and it
is possible that the additional cost will cause the project to be financially
infeasible.

Methodology
To support an inclusionary requirement, a development project must demonstrate
feasibility in excess of a feasibility “threshold,” described in more detail below.
Based on this criterion, the feasibility analysis is intended to demonstrate if an
inclusionary housing program is an appropriate tool to adopt at this time given
market conditions, and, if so, identify inclusionary requirements that could be
feasibly absorbed by different types of new market-rate projects in the City. The
analysis utilizes information on market rents and sale prices in the City, affordable
rents and sale prices in the region, and development costs for new residential
units in the region. The analysis reflects costs and values of newly constructed
housing units since the IHO only applies to new development projects.

Assumptions
Product Prototypes
The feasibility analysis was conducted on a series of prototype residential
products intended to reflect the types of new residential development projects
expected to occur in the City in the coming years. The prototypes were informed
by EPS research on the local housing market, which included review of recent
developments and proposed projects, discussions with developers active in the
City and subregion, input from City staff, and City zoning regulations.

The analyzed prototypes include three Citywide prototypes, reflecting residential
zoning designations across the City; and three MU Zone prototypes reflecting the
City’s MU zoning designation. Prototypes for the MU Zone are considered
separately as the MU designation provides zoning allowances distinct from other
residential zones in the City. Specifically, there is no limit on density for projects
in the MU Zone. Additionally, many of the properties located in the MU Zone meet
the requirements of California law, which allows a developer to provide fewer
parking spaces than required by the City standards if the development is
constructed within ½ miles of a major transit hub. Since the MU Zone is expected
to absorb a significant amount of future residential development in the City, it is

particularly important to understand the impact of the IHO on future projects in
the MU Zone area.

The Citywide prototypes include one rental prototype – multifamily apartments –
and two for-sale prototypes – multifamily condominiums and attached
townhomes. The critical differentiator between the two for-sale prototypes is the
density at which they are built, with the “condominium” product assumed to be
built at a density of 30 units per acre and the “townhome” product assumed to be
built at a density of 20 units per acre. These densities align with zoning
regulations for the City’s R-2 and R-3 zones, and the associated product types are
based on how units at those densities can fit on a site. Given these densities, it is
assumed that the condominium units would be contained within a single multi-
story building, while the townhome units would be built as distinct units, each
with its own ground-floor entrance (although likely with shared walls). The
analysis also assumes that the prototypical condominium units are smaller than
the prototypical townhome unit. While there may be additional factors – such as
how the lot is subdivided – that the City uses to define a project as a
condominium or townhome, this analysis does not account for those types of
factors and only differentiates the prototypes based on density and unit size.

The Mixed-Use prototypes include two rental multifamily apartment prototypes
and one for-sale multifamily condominium prototype. These products reflect
characteristics of pipeline projects currently seen in the MU Zone. The difference
between the two rental prototypes is the parking ratios, with one prototype
assuming 2 spaces per unit and the other prototype assuming 1.5 spaces per unit.
The two rental prototypes were developed per guidance from staff in the City’s
Community Development Department to reflect the range of parking ratios
anticipated in pipeline and future projects. The Mixed-Use for-sale multifamily
condominium prototype (for both market-rate and affordable units) also reflects a
lower parking ratio of 2 spaces per unit as compared to the corresponding
Citywide prototype, which assumes a parking ratio of 2.5 spaces per unit. 7

The unit characteristics for each prototype are meant to represent average unit
sizes, with the resulting analysis demonstrating feasibility for an average
residential project. The findings of this analysis assume that the unique unit mix
of any particular project will, in aggregate, conform to these average unit sizes.
However, any specific project will have its own cost and revenue factors that may
be impacted in part by its unit mix. Additionally, this analysis does not include a
detached single-family home prototype, as the City anticipates limited future
development of this product type.

Value Assumptions
Market-Rate Residential Values
The value for market-rate rental apartments is based on annual net operating
income (NOI), which is calculated as annual rent minus annual operating
expenses. For the apartment prototypes in Monterey Park, annual rent is assumed
at $33,420 per unit (equivalent to $2,785 per month), and annual operating
expenses are assumed at $10,000 per unit. This rental rate reflects market rents
for newly constructed apartment projects in the San Gabriel Valley subregion.

For the market-rate for-sale prototypes, the value of the unit is equal to the
estimated sale price. The assumed price points for new for-sale products in
Monterey Park are $674,000 for a condominium unit and $870,000 for a
townhome unit. These price points reflect expectations for newly constructed
units, which are assumed to achieve higher prices than the overall existing
inventory. For this analysis, EPS applied a premium of 40 percent over existing
inventory values to estimate projected prices for new units, based on sales trend
data for the San Gabriel Valley subregion.

Affordable Residential Values
Affordable rents and sale prices for inclusionary units are based on maximum
housing costs affordable to households at various household income levels.
Income levels for households in Los Angeles County are set by California law on
an annual basis. The income level for each category differs by household size.
This analysis assumes a two-bedroom unit is occupied by a three-person
household and a three-bedroom unit is occupied by a four-person household. 8 For
2023, the Area Median Income (AMI) in Los Angeles County is defined as $88,400
for a household of three and $98,200 for a household of four.

In general, Very Low-Income households are defined as those earning up to
50 percent of AMI; Low-Income households earn up to 80 percent AMI; and
Moderate-Income households earn up to 120 percent of AMI. However, within
Los Angeles County, the maximum income defining Very Low- and Low-Income
households is adjusted upwards from the associated percentage of AMI. This
adjustment occurs in counties with relatively high housing costs and/or relatively
high or low household incomes. Due to this adjustment, the maximum income for
a Low-Income household—$90,850 for a three-person household and $100,900
for a four-person household—is actually higher than the area median income.

Feasibility Thresholds
The assessment of financial feasibility for real estate development products is
based on calculating financial return metrics for the products and comparing them
against typical industry target thresholds. In the case of residential development,
relevant return metrics are based on comparing total project revenues to total
project development costs, as follows:

•  For for-sale market-rate housing prototypes, which in this analysis includes
  condominiums and townhomes, the estimated cost of development (shown in
  Table 5, Table 6, and Table 9) is subtracted from the estimated value, or
  sale price, in order to calculate profit. The profit is then divided by the
  estimated development cost to calculate the relevant feasibility metric, profit
  margin, which is the percentage by which total project value exceeds total
  project cost. Based on EPS research and feedback from the developer
  community, the analysis assumes that developers in the greater Los Angeles
  region will require a projected profit margin of at least 15 percent to move
  forward with a for-sale development project. Therefore, a prototype attaining
  a profit margin at or above 15 percent at market sale prices would be
  considered feasible in this analysis. A profit margin in excess of 15 percent
  would be required to support any additional costs, such as an inclusionary
  requirement.

•  For rental market-rate housing prototypes, which in this analysis includes
  multifamily apartments, the feasibility threshold is based on the return metric
  of “yield on cost,” which is calculated by dividing the annual net operating
  income (NOI) by the total costs of development. 9 Based on EPS research and
  experience, the analysis assumes that developers in the greater Los Angeles
  region will require a projected yield on cost of at least 5.5 percent in order to
  move forward with a multifamily rental development project. A yield-on-cost
  in excess of 5.5 percent would be required to support any additional costs,
  such as an inclusionary requirement.

It is important to note that these return metrics do not account for the time value
of money and are not based on any assumption regarding project timeline.

As shown, the analysis indicates that only the townhome prototype both meets

multifamily prototypes achieve feasible return thresholds at market rates,
although the Mixed-Use prototypes’ higher densities and lower parking ratios
increase revenue and lower development cost, and are therefore estimated to
generate higher returns as compared to their Citywide counterparts. Overall, the
estimated returns for the multifamily prototypes suggest that, on average, it is
challenging to develop these project types in the City under current market

those challenges and potentially limit the opportunities for new housing
development in the community.

It is important to note that this analysis only reflects average prototypical projects
and does not mean that the prototypes shown as infeasible above will never be
built in the City. There are many factors that can impact the financial feasibility of
any particular development project. For example, if a project can acquire land at a
lower price or build at a higher density than what is represented in the above
assumptions, the project may become financially feasible. Similarly, a developer
may find that there is sufficient demand to achieve rents or sale prices higher
than those assumed in this analysis. Indeed, the City may find that even though
this analysis shows specific types of development to be infeasible at market rates,
they still receive proposals to build these types of projects. Therefore, as stated
previously in this report, the analysis should not be considered deterministic
regarding the future of housing development in the City. Rather, it should be
taken as informative regarding the obstacles to housing development under
current average market conditions, and how inclusionary housing requirements
might therefore impact the feasibility of the average project.

4. In-Lieu Fee Calculation
In addition to evaluating the impacts of the City’s IHO on development feasibility,
EPS was scoped to calculate an in-lieu fee that developers might pay instead of
providing affordable units on-site. The City adopted a resolution in September
2023 regarding calculation of the in-lieu fee, which called for the fee to equal “the
difference between the market rate price and the defined affordable price…
associated with each income restricted unit required to be produced.”10 While this
is one possible approach for calculating an in-lieu fee, EPS recommends an
alternative approach that would still reflect the City’s goal to establish a fee that
reflects “the financial impact or ‘affordability gap’ that is created by the IHO,” and
is commonly used in other jurisdictions across the State. 11

In EPS’s recommended approach, the in-lieu fee is set to equal (as closely as
possible) the cost that developers incur in providing on-site affordable units. This
cost manifests as a “financial gap” associated with inclusionary units, calculated
as the cost of developing the inclusionary unit (which is the same as the cost to
build a market-rate unit) minus the inclusionary unit’s value based on maximum
affordable rents or sales prices. The in-lieu fee per required affordable unit would
be based on that financial gap.

gap for each modeled prototype unit at values associated with Low- and
Moderate-Income affordability levels. The calculation utilizes the development

Given these findings, EPS has outlined several strategies for the City to consider
regarding the immediate and long-term future of the IHO. These strategies can
help the City balance its affordable housing objectives with current market and
development feasibility conditions. These strategies are not necessarily mutually
exclusive, and the City may decide to pursue them in combination.

1. Temporarily pause the inclusionary housing requirement. The City may
  consider a pause in enforcement of the IHO until there is more market
  evidence that the development economics of residential development,
  particularly multifamily development, are improving. The City can continue to
  monitor several metrics in this regard, including developer interest and
  applications, residential production trends, development costs, and market
  prices/rents in the City. A reasonable timeframe for monitoring changing real
  estate and financial markets conditions would be one to two years. When
  early indicators, such as increased developer interest and multifamily rents,
  suggest improving market conditions, the City may then reevaluate the
  feasibility of its inclusionary program. While it would be a “best practice” to
  conduct another feasibility study at that time, the law does not require it.

2. Phase-in the IHO requirements. It can take some time for the market to
  respond to new inclusionary requirements and for developers to figure out
  how to adjust their development programs to maintain feasibility. Sometimes
  phasing in inclusionary requirements is a way for a jurisdiction to signal to the
  development community what is coming while allowing projects already in
  early planning stages to respond.

  A phase-in approach has been used in several jurisdictions, including in the
  cities of Long Beach and San Jose, as described below:

-  The City of Long Beach phased in its inclusionary requirements over a three-
  year period, starting in 2021. Ownership projects that submitted their
  application for first approval in the first year were required to include 4
  percent of units as affordable to Moderate-Income households. Those applying
  in the second year had to include 5 percent of units as affordable, and those
  applying in the third year had to include 10 percent of units as affordable.
  Similarly, for rental projects, applicants in the first year had to include 5
  percent of units as affordable to Very-Low Income households, with the
  requirements increasing to 6 percent and then 11 percent for applicants in the
  second and third years. The City’s in-lieu fee levels were similarly phased in.

-  In San Jose, the City adopted its inclusionary housing ordinance in early
  2010 but delayed implementation until 2013. The City also added a market-
  based “trigger” to allow for earlier implementation if the housing market
  picked up more quickly than expected. Specifically, the ordinance could go
  into effect if at least 2,500 building permits were issued within a 12-month
  consecutive period.

3. Adjust the housing requirements so that the complying projects
  automatically qualify for the State Density Bonus (SDB). As written, the
  City’s inclusionary requirement for for-sale projects qualifies developers for a
  10 percent density bonus through the SDB. For rental projects, the City’s
  current inclusionary requirements do not automatically align with
  requirements for using the SDB. However, if the City increases the current
  requirement of 9 percent of units for Low Income households to 10 percent of
  units, projects would automatically qualify for a 20 percent density bonus. The
  City could potentially eliminate the requirement for Moderate-Income housing
  on rental to offset the cost of the additional Low-Income requirement. While
  this adjustment to the rental inclusionary requirements may not completely
  resolve feasibility concerns under current market conditions, the additional
  density and other regulatory waivers and concessions allowed under the SDB
  have economic value and can improve the feasibility of a residential project.

4. Consider adopting an in-lieu fee that is lower than the equivalent
  subsidy of providing units on-site. This would lessen the cost burden on
  developers while still generating revenue for City to use specifically for
  affordable housing initiatives and opportunities. Some examples of cities that
  have implemented such a strategy include Jurupa Valley and San Clemente.

  In taking this approach, the City should anticipate that most developers will
  choose to pay the in-lieu fee. However, even under this approach, some
  developers may still choose to build affordable units on-site anyway to qualify
  for the extra density and the waivers/concessions available under the SDB,
  which may be even more valuable to their project.

  If the City does take this approach, it may still only be helpful to the
  developers of attached townhome projects under current market conditions.
  Given the feasibility challenges demonstrated for multifamily development at
  market rates, even an in-lieu fee that is set below the equivalent cost of the
  on-site inclusionary requirement (e.g., $2 to $5 per square foot) may be more
  cost than new projects of this type can absorb at this time.

  It is also important to note that while cities do not often take this approach at
  the outset of establishing a new inclusionary housing program, it tends to
  happen over time if cities do not regularly update their inclusionary housing
  in-lieu fees. For example, cities that have not updated their in-lieu fees in
  some time may find that the cost to a developer of complying with the
  inclusionary requirement by building affordable units on-site far exceeds the
  cost of paying the in-lieu fee, given changes in development costs over time.

While the above strategies will not change the market and economic conditions
impacting residential development projects, they can reduce the additional costs
associated with inclusionary requirements. This in turn may increase the
likelihood that any individual market-rate project can feasibly contribute to the
supply of affordable units in the City.

  bonds back to the City at a discount, the City could generate debt service savings
  with the repurchase of 2021 POBS.

5-A.  PROVIDE AN UPDATE AND RECOMMENDATIONS REGARDING THE
  MONTEREY PARK REWARDS PROGRAM

  Staff anticipates that the existing $60,000 budget allocation for the MPK Rewards
  program app will be fully expended before the end of the calendar year, December
  2023. Should the City Council wish to continue with a shop local reward app
  through June 30, 2024, an additional $60,000 budget appropriation will be
  required. Due to the MPK rewards app’s high operating costs and limitations on
  translating the smartphone-based application to Chinese and Spanish, the
  Economic Development staff researched other platforms, allowing the City to
  provide a customer rewards program for local businesses. The City Council may
  consider appropriating additional funds to transition to a more cost-effective and
  translatable alternative with Bludot’s Open Rewards app.

  Staff asks that the City Council provide direction to staff regarding a shop local
  program. Option One, this report compares the two shop-local programs: MPK

RECOMMENDATION:

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):

Adoption of the Resolution is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act
(“CEQA”) under CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) because it can be seen with certainty
that there is no possibility that the action proposed by the proposed resolution would have
a significant effect on the environment.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

Adopting the attached resolution will allow the City to recover costs, including attorney’s
fees, incurred the City’s abatement of the public nuisance present on certain real property
located in the City (Lot 1 of Tract No. 34875—APN 5254-002-031) (the “Property”) owned
by Center Int’l Investments, Inc. (“CII”). The Resolution authorizes recording the
associated Notice of Nuisance Abatement Lien in the amount of $3,683,075.89. This will
be the sixth lien placed on the Property and covers expenses that the City incurred
between July 1, 2023, and September 30, 2023. After recording this lien, the liens against
the Property will total $15,776,980.16.

BACKGROUND AND DISCUSSION:

As the Council is aware, the City is abating the public nuisance on the Property in
accordance with the Settlement Agreement voluntarily entered into by CII in the civil case
captioned The People of the State of California, ex rel., Mark D. Hensley, City Attorney
for the City of Monterey Park v. Center Int’l Investments, Inc., et al. which was filed on
December 31, 2015 (LASC Case No. BC605788).

On May 4, 2022, and August 1, 2022, March 15, 2023, and September 3, 2023, the City
authorized liens against the Property for nuisance abatement cost recovery. On
November 21, 2023, Management Services Director Martha Garcia sent correspondence
(Resolution Exhibit A) demanding CII’s payment of $3,683,075.89 to the City in
abatement costs for Quarter 3 of 2023. This is in addition to liens already placed on the
Property totaling $12,093,904.27. The City has not received any payments from CII. After
recording this lien, the liens against the Property will total $15,776,980.16.

Pursuant to MPMC § 4.30.150 and Government Code § 38773.1, the City may recover

Property. Under California law and upon recordation, the notice would constitute a lien
against the Property with the force, effect, and priority of a judgment lien. The City can
foreclose against the lien through an action for a money judgment. CII previously agreed
to waive its notice and hearing rights in § 7 of the First Amendment to the Settlement
Agreement.

of $3,683,075.89. This is one of several notices that will be continuing being brought to

SECTION 4: Zone Change Findings. Pursuant to MPMC §§ 21.38.050 and 21.42.010,
the City Council finds as follows:

A.  The zone change is consistent with the goals, policies and objectives of the
  General Plan and will create consistency between the General Plan Land Use
  designations and zone designations on the Zoning Map. The zone change affects
  areas that have a voter approved Land Use designation that implements the
  Monterey Park Land Use and Urban Design Element (Measure JJ). The
  correlations between the proposed zone changes and General Plan Land Use
  designations exist as follows:

  (1)  The Monterey Park Land Use and Urban Design Element identifies
  Innovation/Technology designation as an area for primary uses related to
  research and development, light manufacturing, service commercials,
  professional offices, entertainment, and breweries/wineries/distilleries. The
  Monterey Park Land Use and Urban Design Element also identifies retail
  and service commercial uses as support services within the
  Innovation/Technology designation.

  (2)  Monterey Park Land Use and Urban Design Element Policy 24.1 seeks to
  ensure that zoning regulations applicable to the Monterey Pass Road
  corridor permit the range of uses necessary to achieve land use goals and
  prohibit uses that conflict with those goals.

  (3)  The S-C – Shopping Center zone provides for the development of shopping
  and business centers that serve as major retail attraction for the broader
  community.

  (4)  The O-P – Office Professional zone provides for the development of
  integrated professional, office and limited retail areas that exhibit a diversity
  of business activity.

  (5)  The Monterey Park Land Use and Urban Design Element identifies High
  Density designation as an area for primary uses that include attached or
  detached residential units, with private common open space, at densities
  ranging from 16.1 to 30 units per acre.

  (6)  The C-S – Commercial Services zone provides for the development of
  commercial areas that promote retail and provide transition areas between
  the City and neighboring communities.

  (7)  The R-3 – High Density Residential zone provides high density residential
  housing either attached or detached multiple-family units at a density of 25
  units per acre.

B.  The zone change will not adversely affect surrounding properties, as the types of

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The City recently began efforts in the Our City, Our Plan campaign to implement the
General Plan Land Use and Urban Design Element (“GPLU”) and the Housing Element
(“HE”), which sets the vision for development within the City. The General Plan is
implemented through the zoning regulations located in Title 21 of the Monterey Park
Municipal Code (“MPMC”). Those regulations assign a zoning district to each property in
the City, as governed by the Zoning Map. This proposed zone change will harmonize the
zoning designations with the GPLU for certain properties on Monterey Pass Road,
Corporate Center Drive and East Mabel Avenue.

The Zone Changes will only impact the future development of these properties; existing
structures and businesses are allowed to remain.

  The City Council ordains as follows:

SECTION 1. The City Council finds and determines as follows:

  A.  Article XI, § 7 of the California Constitution empowers the City to enact
  and enforce ordinances regulating conditions that may be public
  nuisances or health hazards, or that promote social, economic, or
  aesthetic considerations.

  B.  The Federal Controlled Substances Act, 21 U.S.C. § 801, et seq.,
  classifies cannabis as a Schedule 1 Drug, which is defined as a drug or
  other substance that has a high potential for abuse, that has no currently
  accepted medical use in treatment in the United States, and that has not
  been accepted as safe for use under medical supervision. The Federal
  Controlled Substances Act makes it unlawful under federal law for any
  person to cultivate, manufacture, distribute or dispense, or possess with
  intent to manufacture, distribute or dispense, cannabis.

  C.  The penalties for violating federal law include fines between $10,000 and
  $50,000 (21 U.S.C. § 841) for first time offenders. California law has
  similar provisions (see, e.g., Health and Safety Code §§ 11352 and
  11379.6).

  D.  As of the effective date of this Ordinance, the City Council has not
  authorized any cannabis activity within its jurisdiction. To the contrary,
  Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) § 6.35.030 explicitly prohibits all
  commercial cannabis activity in the City including, without limitation,
  medical cannabis dispensaries and medical cannabis delivery services.

  E.  A statewide initiative entitled the “Control, Regulate and Tax Adult Use of
  Marijuana Act” (“AUMA”) was approved by voters on the November 2016
  ballot. AUMA does not, and cannot, affect federal regulations as to
  cannabis or its derivatives.

  F.  AUMA expressly preserves local control over the regulation of cannabis-
  related businesses and cannabis-related land uses (Business &
  Professions Code § 26200, et seq.).

  G.  In City of Riverside v. Inland Empire Patients Health and Wellness Center,
  Inc. (2013) 56 Cal.4th 729, the California Supreme Court held that nothing

  in state cannabis law “expressly or impliedly limits the inherent authority of
  a local jurisdiction, by its own ordinances, to regulate the use of its land[.]”
  Additionally, in Maral v. City of Live Oak (2013) 221 Cal.App.4th 975, the
  Court of Appeal held that “there is no right – and certainly no constitutional
  right – to cultivate medical marijuana[.]” The Court in Maral affirmed the
  ability of a local governmental entity to prohibit the cultivation of cannabis
  under its land use authority.

  H.  It is in the public interest for the City to take appropriate actions to protect
  citizens and their property from conditions that threaten public health,
  safety, and welfare including, without limitation, matters that devalue real
  property.

  I.  On September 18, 2022, Governor Newsom signed Senate Bill (“SB”)
  1186, known as the “Medicinal Cannabis Patients’ Right of Access Act”
  into law.

  J.  SB 1186 imposes restrictions on how cities may regulate the retail sale by
  delivery of medical cannabis within their jurisdiction.

  K.  The City Council is required by California law to enact this Ordinance to
  regulate how qualified delivery-only medical cannabis retailers may

  L.  On November 30, 2023, the Planning Commission recommended that the

The California Legislature adopted Senate Bill 1886 (“SB 1186”) in 2022 which precludes
cities from imposing regulations that have the effect of prohibiting medical cannabis
delivery within the City and becomes effective on January 1, 2024. SB 1186 declares that
any City regulation that does not allow a physical premises from which retail sale by
delivery of medical cannabis may be conducted within the City has the effect of prohibiting
medical cannabis delivery. Accordingly, the proposed ordinance will conditionally allow
non-store front locations for the sale by delivery of medical cannabis in the Commercial
Services Zone and impose reasonable regulations.

BACKGROUND:

SB 1186 (2022) is intended to increase access to medical cannabis. The California
Legislature stated that access to medical cannabis has been adversely impacted by the
Medicinal and Adult Use Cannabis Regulation and Safety Act, which gave cities the ability
to ban all cannabis activity, including medical cannabis.

The MPMC currently prohibits all commercial cannabis facilities, including medical
cannabis. MPMC § 6.35.030 prohibits all “commercial cannabis activity” within the City.
“Commercial cannabis activity” is defined as the “cultivation, possession, manufacture,
processing, storing, laboratory testing, labeling, transporting, distribution, or sale of
cannabis or a cannabis product.” MPMP § 6.35.040 defines a cannabis “facility” to include
“medical marijuana collective[s].” Medical marijuana dispensaries are also prohibited in
residential zones by MPMPC § 21.08.030.

ANALYSIS

Pursuant to SB 1186, a City may not impose regulation of any of the following type that
has the effect of prohibiting the retail sale by delivery of medical cannabis:

  1.  The number of medical cannabis businesses authorized to deliver medical
cannabis in the local jurisdiction.

  2.  The operating hours of medical cannabis businesses.

  3.  The number or frequency of sales by delivery of medical cannabis.

  4.  The types or quantities of medical cannabis authorized to be sold by
delivery.

  5.  The establishment of physical premises from which retail sale by delivery
of medical cannabis within the jurisdiction is conducted by a licensed non-storefront
retailer.

However, SB 1186 allows the City to impose reasonable regulations on the retail sale by
delivery of medical cannabis through the City’s police powers. Therefore, the City can
adopt or enforce reasonable regulations on the non-storefront retail delivery of medical
cannabis related to:

  1.  Zoning requirements.

  2.  Security or public health and safety requirements.

  3.  Licensing requirements.

  4.  Imposing or collecting applicable state or local taxes on retail sales of
medical cannabis occurring within the City.

  5.  Regulations consistent with requirements or restrictions imposed on
cannabis businesses by California law or regulations promulgated by the Department of
Cannabis Control.

The proposed Ordinances will ensure that the MPMC is compliant with California law
concerning medical cannabis effective on January 1, 2024, by:

  1.  Repealing MPMC § 9.102 (Medical Marijuana) which referenced a non-
existent section of the MPMC;

  2.  Amending MPMC § 6.35.030 (Prohibition) to add a clause stating that all
commercial cannabis activity is prohibited “without the permits required by this code”;

  3.  Adding a new Chapter 6.36 to the MPMC (Medical Cannabis Delivery)
which imposes operational standards on physical premises from which retail sale by
delivery of medical cannabis is conducted;

clarify that “no new use is permitted unless permitted by both State and Federal law”;

  5.  Repealing MPMC § 21.04.557 (Marijuana) which defined marijuana;

  6.  Repealing MPMC § 21.04.571 (Medical Marijuana Dispensary) which
defined “medical marijuana dispensaries”; and

  7.  Adding Chapter 21.27 (Cannabis-Related Uses) to the MPMC to establish

Overall, the proposed Ordinances, if adopted, help to achieve goals and objectives set by

(upon 4/5 vote) that would take effect immediately. Additionally, the City Council would
introduce a regular ordinance; adoption would be scheduled for the regular January 17,

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The City received a petition to designate a preferential parking district along E. Hellman
Avenue from N. Alhambra Avenue to N. Nicholson Avenue. Staff investigated the
proposed parking district and the surrounding street parking conditions. It is
recommended that City Council adopt a resolution designating E. Hellman Avenue from
N. Alhambra Avenue to N. Nicholson Avenue as a preferential parking district.

BOARD/COMMISSION REVIEW:
On August 17, 2023, staff presented the request for a permit parking district on E. Hellman
Avenue from N. Alhambra Avenue to N. Nicholson Avenue to the Traffic Commission.
Staff provided an overview of the request and survey findings which did not support the
establishment of a parking district. It was recommended that additional monitoring be
conducted as the parking surveys were completed during the time that the neighboring
school, Mark Keppel High School, was not in session. On October 19, staff presented the
results of the secondary monitoring and recommended that the City Council designate a
preferential parking district along E. Hellman Avenue from N. Alhambra Avenue to N.
Nicholson Avenue.

BACKGROUND
On December 6, 2023 the City adopted Ordinance 2238, amending the Monterey Park
Municipal Code (“MPMC”) by adding Chapter 10.68 entitled “Preferential Parking Permits”
which provides a process for residents to petition the City to establish a permit parking
area, and the criteria for considering residential parking districts.

The residents of E. Hellman Avenue from N. Alhambra Avenue to N. Nicholson Avenue
petitioned the City for the establishment of a preferential parking area due to the excess
number of vehicles from outside of the neighborhood taking up limited street parking. The
petition included signatures from ten residents occupying the twelve dwelling unitswithin
the proposed parking area. This meets the minimum 66% requirement that the petition
be signed by not less than residents living in at least 66% of the dwelling units in the
proposed specified area.

E. Hellman Avenue is considered a local roadway and it is approximately 32 feet wide
with one travel lane in each direction and parking on both sides of the road. Hellman
Avenue North of the centerline is in the City of Alhambra right of way. Parking is allowed
on the proposed street segment at all times except on Thursdays from 8:00 a.m. to noon
due to street sweeping and two existing 20-feet of red curb at both ends of the proposed
segments. Land use along the studied segment is multi-family residential. Designation
as a permit parking area may provide practical and convenient parking benefits to the
residents and add to their quality of life. All of the properties fronting the proposed
segment of Hellman have on-site parking, with long driveways. The City of Alhambra
does not allow overnight parking on city streets, so it is common for Alhambra residents
to park on Monterey Park streets.

Staff performed monitoring upon receipt of the petition for permit parking. However, the
results of the initial monitoring did not support the petition. It was recommended that
additional monitoring be conducted as the parking surveys were completed during the
time that the neighboring school, Mark Keppel High School, was not in session. Additional
monitoring of cars parked along the proposed segment was conducted at various times
of the day and night when school was back in session and it was determined that during
70% of the days evaluated, 50% or more of the cars parked along the studied segment
were out of the area. In addition, the field monitoring determined that throughout the
overall study, 62% of the cars during the monitoring were out of the area.

If approved by the City Council, the proposed parking district on E. Hellman Avenue would
restrict parking 24 hours a day, seven days a week adjacent to the residential area. The
limits of the permit parking will start from N. Alhambra Avenue to N. Nicholson Avenue.

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Approving the list of haulers qualified to submit proposals for a waste collection
  and recycling franchise for residential and/or commercial services;
  2. Authorizing the release of the Request for Applications (RFA) to the list of qualified
  haulers; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On October 18, 2023 the City Council approved the release of a Request for Qualifications
(RFQ) as the first step to solicit proposals for new solid waste franchise agreements. Ten
companies responded to the RFQ and submitted Statements of Qualifications (SOQ).
With the assistance of HF&H consultants, the City evaluated the SOQs and determined
that eight companies are qualified to apply for both a residential franchise and a
commercial franchise.

It is recommended that City Council approve the list of qualified haulers and authorize the
release of the Request for Applications (RFA) for a waste collection and recycling
franchise.

BACKGROUND:
Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) Chapter 6.09 requires the City to award solid
waste franchises on a competitive basis. The City contracted with HF&H consultants for
assistance with the solid waste Request for Applications (“RFA”) and new solid waste
contracts. The RFQ was the first step in a four-step process leading to the selection of
one or more franchisees to provide waste management services in the City.

  Step 1:  Interested companies submit statements of qualification to the City.
  Step 2:  The City evaluates the submittals and develops a list of qualified
  companies.

  Step 3:  The qualified companies are invited to submit applications and
  service rates for a residential franchise, a commercial franchise, or
  both.
  Step 4:  The City evaluates the applications in relation to the stated criteria
  and selects the companies to be awarded franchises to the lowest
  bidders that are willing to execute the City’s contracts.

On October 18, 2023 the City Council approved the release of a Request for Qualifications
(RFQ) for new residential and commercial waste collection and recycling franchises that
included the following qualification criteria:

  The company must be currently providing waste collection, recycling, and disposal
  services in at least three franchise areas in California. If the company desires to
  be considered for a residential franchise in Monterey Park, it must be currently
  providing services relatively similar to those described in the residential service
  plan in at least three residential franchise areas in California. If the company
  desires to be considered for a commercial franchise in Monterey Park, it must be
  currently providing services relatively similar to those described in the commercial
  service plan in at least three commercial franchise areas in California. These
  franchises must have been awarded by a California city, county, regional agency
  that provides waste services, or municipal service agency or district.

The residential service plan includes, without limitation, the weekly collection, recycling,
and disposal of waste from approximately 14,000 single-family and multifamily residences
either through a 2-cart system (Mixed Waste and Mixed Organics) or 3-cart system
(Refuse, Recyclable materials, and Mixed Organics); diversion of at least 50% of refuse
materials collected through approved CalRecycle diversion methods; provision of labeled
containers to customers; provision of collection services for four cleanup events per year,
billing customers for services on a bi-monthly basis; bulky item collection; and customer
outreach and education.

The commercial service plan includes, without limitation, the collection, recycling, and
disposal of waste from approximately 1,000 commercial and industrial businesses in the
City; diversion of at least 50% of refuse materials collected through approved CalRecycle
diversion methods and at least 65% of construction and demolition debris; disposal of
non-recyclable waste at fully-permitted disposal facilities; provision of labeled containers
to customers; provision of collection services for City facilities and public containers;
billing customers for services; and customer outreach and education.

Both the residential and commercial service plans also include services in compliance
with California law and CalRecycle regulations such as contamination monitoring; route
reviews and inspections; food recovery assistance; waiver assistance; organic waste
recovery education and outreach; recordkeeping and reporting requirements; and
Recovered Organic Waste Product (ROWP) Procurement.

MPMC § 6.09.070 states that "the city council must award any franchise based upon the
applicant proposing the lowest proposed monthly rates to the customer." The proposed
RFA includes forms to be completed by the applicants that will automatically calculate
each applicant's monthly rate for each service level, thereby providing the City Council
with a basis for awarding the franchises.

The program parameters specified in the RFA are as follows:

    An exclusive franchise will be awarded for residential waste collection and
  recycling services.
    Either a single exclusive or up to three non-exclusive franchises will be awarded
  for commercial waste collection and recycling services.
    The term of all franchises will be seven years with no renewals.
    Customer rates can be adjusted annually by the change in the Consumer Price
  Index for all urban consumers in Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim area.
    Haulers can submit proposals for a 2-cart or 3-cart system for residential and
  commercial customers.
    Franchisees must achieve and maintain a waste diversion rate of at least 50%,
  using CalRecycle’s per capita generation and Disposal data.

A copy of the proposed franchise agreement for the residential program and the
commercial program will be distributed with the RFA. Final agreements will be in a form
approved by the City Attorney.

2023-2024 STRATEGIC PLAN GOAL:
The RFA meets the City’s goal of Sustainability. Awarding franchise agreements to
qualified waste management companies provides the City with oversight and regulation
of the collection, storage, transportation, processing, and disposal of refuse, recyclables,
and construction and demolition debris. This not only ensures the City meets state
requirements but also supports the City’s continued success of recycling and organic
waste diversion programs.

FISCAL IMPACT:
There is no fiscal impact in approving the list of qualified haulers nor the release of the
RFA.

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and Filing the staff report summarizing the status of emergency repairs
  to the Monterey Pass Road water line; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

BACKGROUND:
On August 17, 2022, City Council adopted Resolution No. 2022-R69 authorizing the City
Manager to take necessary measures for emergency repair of a water main line on
Monterey Pass Road. Recurring water main leaks in several areas within Monterey Pass
Road between the intersections of Vagabond Drive and Brightwood Street resulted in
extensive infrastructure damage to the roadway and necessary water main pipe repairs
to ensure continued water service to residences and businesses in the area.

The design phase was completed in December 2022 followed by research of available
material and cost in December 2022 and January 2023 to ensure the project could be
expedited due to the significant material delivery delays. Construction started in March
2023 and was completed by December 2023.

As part of the City’s outreach efforts, the construction manager visited businesses along
the project area prior to the start of the project to notify them of the upcoming construction.
The Economic Development Division also mailed out letters to businesses that may be
impacted by this project. Message boards were placed within the project area prior to
construction commencing to alert drivers of the impact to their commutes.

The construction portion of the project is 100% complete. The contractor has:
  x Installed the 12-inch pipeline for the entire project from Floral Drive to Vagabond
  Road for a total length of 10,800 linear feet of pipeline;
  x Installed all interconnecting pipes including the connection at Vagabond Road;
  x Installed all the lateral pipelines for the water services, fire services, and fire
  hydrants for the project;
  x Completed hydrostatic pressure testing of the pipeline.

  AGENDA ITEM NO: Public Hearing - 4A

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council

 FROM:  Karl H. Berger, City Attorney

 SUBJECT:  Continued Public Hearing to consider adopting an Ordinance
  Incorporating by Reference Chapter 7.46 of Los Angeles County Code
  Title 7 – Business Licenses into a new Chapter 5.90 of the Monterey
  Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”)

RECOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council consider:

  1. Opening the continued public hearing to receive both written and oral testimony,
  closing the continued public hearing;
  2. Waiving second reading and adopting an Ordinance that would incorporate by
  reference Los Angeles County Code Title 7, Chapter 7.46 regarding the regulation
  of gun dealers within the City of Monterey Park (“City”); and
  3. Taking such additional, related action that may be desirable.

CEQA DETERMINATION

This Ordinance is exempt from review under the California Environmental Quality Act
(California Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq., “CEQA”) and CEQA Guidelines (14
California Code of Regulations §§ 15000, et seq.) in that it is not a “project” for purposes
of CEQA, as that term is defined by CEQA Guidelines § 15378. Specifically, this
Ordinance constitutes creation of government regulations which do not involve any
commitment to any specific project which may result in a potentially significant physical
impact on the environment. In addition, this Ordinance is an organizational or
administrative activity that will not result in a direct or indirect physical change in the
environment.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

On December 20, 2023, the City Council introduced and waived first reading of an
ordinance, if adopted, would add a new Chapter to the Monterey Park Municipal Code
(“MPMC”) requiring gun dealers to acquire a police permit to operate within the City of
Monterey Park. The City Council continued the scheduled public hearing to the January
17, 2024 council meeting.

  Page 217 of 307
 BACKGROUND

At the December 20, 2023 meeting the City Council was provided with information
regarding the significant strides taken to enhance gun and ammunition regulations within
the City, including the adoption of several resolutions, ordinances, and city policies.

The City Council may wish to adopt an ordinance adding a new Chapter 5.90 to the
MPMC amending the Los Angeles County Code (“LACC”) governing licenses required by
gun dealers within the County’s jurisdiction. The Monterey Park Police Department
(“MPPD”) would then administer the permitting process for gun dealers located within the
City’s jurisdiction.

Revisions to the draft ordinance were made at the December 20, 2023 Council meeting
and those changes have been incorporated into the draft ordinance and is attached to
this staff report.

FISCAL IMPACT

A public hearing regarding permit fees will be scheduled for a future date.

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
 FROM:  Karl H. Berger, City Attorney
 SUBJECT:  An Ordinance Incorporating by Reference Chapter 7.46 of Los Angeles
  County Code Title 7 – Business Licenses into a new Chapter 5.90 of the
  Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”)

RECOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Introducing and waiving first reading, and continuing the scheduled public hearing
  from December 20, 2023 to January 17, 2024 (pursuant to Government Code §
  50022.3) to adopt an Ordinance that would incorporate by reference Los
  Angeles County Code Title 7, Chapter 7.46 regarding the regulation of gun dealers
  within the City of Monterey Park (“City”); and

  2. Take such additional, related action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Since January, the City Council undertook a series of action in response to the mass
shooting that killed 11 individuals and wounded nine others. It was the worst shooting in
Los Angeles County history. In August, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 2023-
R67 which, among other things, gave direction to the City Manager and City Attorney to
take actions needed to support reasonable gun regulation. The draft ordinance, if
adopted, would add a new Chapter to the Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”)
requiring gun dealers to acquire a police permit to operate.

CEQA DETERMINATION

This Ordinance is exempt from review under the California Environmental Quality Act
(California Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq., “CEQA”) and CEQA Guidelines
(14 California Code of Regulations §§ 15000, et seq.) in that it is not a “project” for
purposes of CEQA, as that term is defined by CEQA Guidelines § 15378. Specifically,
this Ordinance constitutes creation of government regulations which do not involve any
commitment to any specific project which may result in a potentially significant physical
impact on the environment. In addition, this Ordinance is an organizational or
administrative activity that will not result in a direct or indirect physical change in the
environment.

  Page 251 of 307
 BACKGROUND

The City Council took significant strides to enhance gun and ammunition regulations
within the City. This includes adopting two ordinances be drafted: one requiring that
trigger locks or storage devices be used for firearms; the other prohibiting firearms on
City-owned property. On August 16, 2023, City Council, in accordance with Section
3(B)(8) of Resolution No. 2023-R15, adopted Ordinance § 9.58.050 entitled “Safe
Storage” to the MPMC. City Council also adopted Resolution No. 2023-R67, declaring
the City Council’s intent to support federal, state, and local gun regulation, including
adopting various city-wide policies and authorizing the City Manager to implement the
City Council’s policies. Resolution No. 2023-R67 declared City Council’s commitment to
lend the City’s support to all reasonable legislation that is intended to protect public
health and safety while maintaining an individual’s constitutional rights as to owning
firearms. In addition, through Resolution No. 2023-R67, City Council approved a pledge
for all elected officials, approved standard conditions of approval for certain conditional
use permits (“CUP”), and authorized the city manager to implement this resolution.
On November 7, 2023, the Los Angeles Board of Supervisors adopted an ordinance
amending the Los Angeles County Code (“LACC”) governing licenses required by gun
dealers within the County’s jurisdiction. LACC Title 7 is comprised of two Divisions:
Division 1 contains the general administrative framework, including application
requirements, processing information, enforcement provisions, and a schedule of fees;
and Division 2 sets forth the specific business licensing requirements and prerequisites
for the business activities the licensed by the County.

A review of the LACC, as amended on November 7th, suggests that the City Council may
wish to incorporate the County regulations into the MPMC by reference. The Monterey
Park Police Department (“MPPD”) would then administer the permitting process for gun
dealers located within the City’s jurisdiction.

The draft Ordinance would add a new Chapter 5.90 to the MPMC that would accomplish
the following:

  •  Requires Gun and Ammunition Dealers apply for a police permit and to
  annually those permits;

  •  Requires security camera systems consistent with the Penal Code;

  •  Restricts minors' presence where guns and ammunition are sold;

  •  Requires signs warning of risks associated with Guns be displayed;

  •  Requires an approved firearm safety device upon delivery of any gun sold,
  leased, or transferred;

  •  Requires Gun and Ammunition Dealers secure and maintain on the business
  premises a record of every gun and ammunition purchaser's thumbprint;

  Page 252 of 307
   •  Requires the maintenance of annual sales reports of Guns and Ammunition
  sold on the business premises for five years and the maintenance of inventory
  in real-time; and

  •  Requires the names of suspended and revoked permittees to be publicly
  posted.

Some of these requirements are duplicative of regulations already adopted by the City
Council.

IMPLEMENTATION OF STRATEGIC PLAN GOALS

The recommended action supports the City’s strong desire to heighten safety standards
and regulations affecting the use and purchase of firearms in the City.

FISCAL IMPACT

A public hearing to set a permit fee will be noticed for January 17, 2023. Any such fees
will offset the costs associated with issuing and enforcing the proposed permits. The
fees are based on full cost recovery and include administration and enforcement of the
program, salaries, employee benefits, indirect costs, and services and supplies.

 SUBJECT:  Requesting direction from the City Council regarding the structure of the
  Sister Cities Commission

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Providing direction to the City Manager regarding the structure of the
  Sister Cities Commission; and
  2. Taking such additional, related action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
Resolution No. 10281 established a Sister Cities Commission in 1998 (Attachment 1). A
subsequent Resolution (No. 10549) added a new sister city (Yeongdeungpo-Gu Seoul,
South Korea) and expanded the Sister Cities Commission membership (Attachment 2).

The Sister Cities Commission is comprised of three members from each Sister Cities
Associations, one of which is the Association President. This Commission operates
differently than the City’s other Commissions, with a set of by-laws developed specifically
for this Commission. In 2013, the City Council exempted the Commission from the
regulations generally governing the City’s boards and commissions in Monterey Park
Municipal Code Chapter 2.82 (Attachment 3).

Representatives from the Sister Cities Commission expressed the desire to continue with
utilizing a separate set of by-laws and board members. The Commission members are
not appointed by City Councilmembers and the Commission is not subject to MPMC
Chapter 2.82, making oversight of the Commission by the City Council challenging. The
City Manager and Recreation and Community Services Director have asked
representatives from the Commission to establish a nonprofit corporation separate from
the City.

Since 2021, the Sister Cities Commission has met five times out of the fifteen scheduled
meetings due to lack of quorum. A quorum for the Sister Cities Commission is defined as
one member from three of the five cities and at least seven members total. The
Commission has not been involved in any of the City’s events or programs and the City

  Page 267 of 307

has looked to the Community Participation Commission for support at City activities. The
Director requested updated information from each of the Sisters City Associations and
found that one of the Associations (Nachikatsurra, Japan) has Active nonprofit status, but
none of them possess General Liability Insurance.

BACKGROUND:
Founded in 1956 by President Eisenhower, Sister Cities International is a non-profit
organization that unites cities worldwide through cultural programs, business
opportunities, and educational exchanges. Monterey Park currently associates itself with
five Sister Cities:

•  Quanzhou, China, Sister City Association
•  Nachikatsurra, Japan, Sister City Association
•  New Taipei City (formerly Yung-Ho) Taiwan, Sister City Association
•  Morelia, Mexico, Sister City Association
•  Yeongdeungpo-Gu, Seoul, South Korea Sister City Association

These associations are independent organizations. In the past, these associations have
planned and implemented student exchange programs and fundraising events. The
stated mission of the Sister Cities Commission includes fostering friendship, goodwill and
communication among the Sister Cities; participating in the exchange of cultures through
events; participating in City of Monterey Park cultural events and programs; and serving
as cultural ambassadors to sister city visitors. Before 2020, the Sister Cities Commission
planned a cultural event/fundraiser, a Mardi Gras event, a Look-A-Like talent show, and
a fundraising dinner.

Since 2021, the City Commission has met five times out of the fifteen scheduled meetings
due to lack of quorum. A quorum for the Sister Cities Commission is defined as one
member from three of the five cities and at least seven members total. The Sister Cities
Commission has not been involved with any City events or programs for several years.

2.  OLD BUSINESS

2-A.  DISCUSSION OF FINDINGS ON CITY’S  INCLUSIONARY  HOUSING
  ORDINANCE FEASIBILITY/FEE STUDY

  On September 6, 2023, the City Council adopted an Inclusionary Housing
  Ordinance (IHO) and an IHO in-lieu fee formula. As part of this action, Council
  also directed the City Manager to conduct an evaluation of the City’s IHO to
  determine whether it is financially feasible and recommend in-lieu fees in cases
  where an IHO is feasible. Based on the Council’s direction, the City partnered with
  the San Gabriel Valley Council of Governments (SGVCOG) and was able to
  participate in SGVCOG’s sub-regional effort to provide technical assistance
  addressing affordable housing issues. The City entered into an agreement with the
  SGVCOG, for its consultant, Economic & Planning Systems (EPS), to conduct an
  IHO feasibility study tailored to Monterey Park.

  EPS’s feasibility study is intended to inform and educate the City Council on the
  potential effects of the IHO on future residential development in the City. The
  study’s overall conclusion states that the requirements of the IHO are likely to be
  financially challenging for new residential development within the City and may
  constrain new projects.

  Public Speakers:

  - Jerry Garner said he is a development consultant with Archivelopment Real
  Estate and is working with a development group in the city that is looking at
  developing a large mixed use or condominium project. He shared that his client
  can’t move forward with the project with the imposition of the affordable housing
  criteria.

  - Oliver Chen, representative of Teamrise LLC, cited the increasing costs
  combined with affordable housing requirements has delayed investment and
  developments. He requested the City Council consider postponing the
  enactment of the Inclusionary Housing Act for a few years so that the housing
  market will be gradually saturated.

  - Selena Zhang said she is a resident, and she feels that this city lacks
  entertainment in comparison to other cities. She encouraged the City Council to
  consider allowing developers to develop more plazas before addressing low
  income housing.

  Discussion: Director of Community Development Serrano introduced Julie
  Cooper and Chinmay Damle, representatives of Economic & Planning Systems
  (EPS), to present a PowerPoint presentation to recite the findings of the IHO
  feasibility study tailored to the City. They were available for questions.
   72-8
  January 17, 2024

  Action Taken: The City Council received and filed the report and presentation
  and directed staff to suspend the IHO for 12 months for further analysis, and to
  report back to the City Council in approximately 9 months with recommendations.

2-B.  LEGISLATIVE SUBPOENAS

  The City Attorney’s office delayed posting a staff report for this item pending
  discussions with TRC’s counsel regarding a City proposal to process land use
  applications utilizing a team of consultants (separate from City staff) paid for by
  TRC.

  TRC accepted this proposal by email dated January 12, 2024 at 10:00 a.m.

  Consequently, it is recommended that the City Council postpone this matter until
  February 21, 2024. This will give TRC and the City enough time to put together
  the reimbursement team and allow the City to assemble the land use team.

  If all elements are in place before February 21, then the legislative subpoena matter
  will be taken off calendar. Staff will instead provide a receive and file item on that
  date regarding the “next steps.”

  Action Taken: The City Council moved this item to be heard and approved as
  part of the Consent Calendar. The City Council continued this matter until the
  regular meeting of February 21, 2024, on Consent Calendar.

2-C.  SR-710 NORTH MOBILITY IMPROVEMENTS PROJECT UPDATE AND
  FUNDING AGREEMENT

  The SR-710 Mobility Improvement Projects are the result of reallocated Measure
  R Funds for the SR-710 North Project to new mobility improvement projects within
  the San Gabriel Valley subregion. These projects are consistent with the purpose
  and need of the Gap Closure Project to relieve congestion on local streets along
  the SR-710 alignment between Interstates 10 and 210, with the highest priority for
  projects proximate to the Interstate 10 freeway. As part of the SR-710 North
  Mobility Improvements Projects, the City received a total allocation of
  $100,300,000 from Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority
  (LACMTA) to complete seven projects.
   72-9
  January 17, 2024

It is recommended that the City Council approve the funding agreement for the
Garvey Avenue Capacity Improvement project which includes a modified scope of
work from the originally proposed project, eliminating the need for adding third
lanes and removal of parking along Garvey Avenue.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
The City reviewed the environmental impacts of the Project under the California
Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and
the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq.,
the “CEQA Guidelines”). CEQA Guidelines §§ 15060(c)(2), 15061(b)(3), and
15378 exempt activities that will not result in a direct or reasonably foreseeable
indirect physical change in the environment, activities where there is possibility that
it may have a significant effect on the environment, and activities that do not
constitute a “project” as defined, respectively. This activity is primarily a legislative
tool to assess legislative and budgetary priorities and does not approve any of the
specific projects for construction, and therefore does not have the potential to have
a significant effect on the environment. Accordingly, no further review is required.
